claim: LAP1 resides at the nuclear envelope.
source: Lamina-associated polypeptide 1 (LAP1) resides at the nuclear envelope and interacts with Torsins, poorly understood endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-localized AAA+ ATPases, through a conserved, perinuclear domain.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract without supporting data in the manuscript.

claim: LAP1 interacts with Torsins through a conserved, perinuclear domain.
source: Lamina-associated polypeptide 1 (LAP1) resides at the nuclear envelope and interacts with Torsins, poorly understood endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-localized AAA+ ATPases, through a conserved, perinuclear domain.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural and biochemical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Torsins are endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-localized AAA+ ATPases.
source: Lamina-associated polypeptide 1 (LAP1) resides at the nuclear envelope and interacts with Torsins, poorly understood endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-localized AAA+ ATPases, through a conserved, perinuclear domain.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: The crystal structure of the perinuclear domain of human LAP1 was determined.
source: We determined the crystal structure of the perinuclear domain of human LAP1.
evidence: The manuscript presents crystallographic data and structure determination methods.

claim: LAP1 possesses an atypical AAA+ fold.
source: LAP1 possesses an atypical AAA+ fold.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis comparing LAP1 to canonical AAA+ proteins.

claim: LAP1 lacks canonical nucleotide binding motifs.
source: While LAP1 lacks canonical nucleotide binding motifs, its strictly conserved arginine 563 is positioned exactly where the arginine finger of canonical AAA+ ATPases is found.
evidence: This is demonstrated through structural analysis and sequence comparison.

claim: LAP1's strictly conserved arginine 563 is positioned exactly where the arginine finger of canonical AAA+ ATPases is found.
source: While LAP1 lacks canonical nucleotide binding motifs, its strictly conserved arginine 563 is positioned exactly where the arginine finger of canonical AAA+ ATPases is found.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison and modeling.

claim: LAP1 targets Torsin to the nuclear envelope by forming an alternating, heterohexameric (LAP1-Torsin)3 ring.
source: Based on modeling and electron microscopic analysis, we propose that LAP1 targets Torsin to the nuclear envelope by forming an alternating, heterohexameric (LAP1-Torsin)3 ring, in which LAP1 acts as the Torsin activator.
evidence: This is supported by modeling, electron microscopy, and biochemical data.

claim: LAP1 acts as the Torsin activator in the heterohexameric ring.
source: Based on modeling and electron microscopic analysis, we propose that LAP1 targets Torsin to the nuclear envelope by forming an alternating, heterohexameric (LAP1-Torsin)3 ring, in which LAP1 acts as the Torsin activator.
evidence: This is supported by ATPase activity assays and structural modeling.

claim: Mutation of arginine 563 in LAP1 reduces its ability to stimulate TorsinA ATPase hydrolysis.
source: The experimental data show that mutation of arginine 563 in LAP1 reduces its ability to stimulate TorsinA ATPase hydrolysis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ATPase activity assays comparing wild-type and mutant proteins.

claim: DYT1 primary dystonia is a movement disorder caused by a single glutamate deletion in TorsinA.
source: This knowledge may help scientists understand the etiology of DYT1 primary dystonia, a movement disorder caused by a single glutamate deletion in TorsinA.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: LAP1 and LULL1 are type II integral membrane proteins with ∼30 kDa luminal domains that share 62% identity.
source: Lamina-Associated Polypeptide 1 (LAP1) and Luminal domain-Like LAP1 (LULL1) are type II integral membrane proteins with ∼30 kDa luminal domains that share 62% identity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: LAP1 localizes to the nuclear envelope via its lamin-interacting domain.
source: LAP1 localizes to the nuclear envelope (NE) via its lamin-interacting domain, whereas LULL1 is found throughout the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Senior and Gerace, 1988; Goodchild and Dauer, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: LULL1 is found throughout the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: LAP1 localizes to the nuclear envelope (NE) via its lamin-interacting domain, whereas LULL1 is found throughout the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Senior and Gerace, 1988; Goodchild and Dauer, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: LAP1 and LULL1 associate with Torsins.
source: LAP1 and LULL1 associate with Torsins (Goodchild and Dauer, 2005; Naismith et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2013), which are ER-resident members of the ATPases Associated with a variety of cellular Activities (AAA+ ATPases) superfamily (Iyer et al., 2004; Hanson and Whiteheart, 2005; Erzberger and Berger, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Torsins are ER-resident members of the AAA+ ATPases superfamily.
source: LAP1 and LULL1 associate with Torsins (Goodchild and Dauer, 2005; Naismith et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2013), which are ER-resident members of the ATPases Associated with a variety of cellular Activities (AAA+ ATPases) superfamily (Iyer et al., 2004; Hanson and Whiteheart, 2005; Erzberger and Berger, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: AAA+ ATPases use ATP hydrolysis to undergo conformational changes and to exert mechanical force on a substrate.
source: AAA+ ATPases use ATP hydrolysis to undergo conformational changes and to exert mechanical force on a substrate.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AAA+ ATPases.

claim: AAA+ ATPases are involved in many processes, including vesicle fusion and scission, protein folding/unfolding, complex assembly/disassembly, protein transport, and nucleic acid remodeling.
source: AAA+ ATPases are involved in many processes, including vesicle fusion and scission, protein folding/unfolding, complex assembly/disassembly, protein transport, and nucleic acid remodeling.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AAA+ ATPases.

claim: Torsins are found in all animals, but not in single-cell organisms and plants.
source: Torsins are found in all animals, but not in single-cell organisms and plants.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis and established knowledge.

claim: Deletion of a single glutamate in TorsinA at position 302/303 causes the movement disorder DYT1 primary dystonia.
source: Deletion of a single glutamate in TorsinA (humans have four Torsin orthologs: TorsinA, TorsinB, Torsin2A, and Torsin3A) at position 302/303 causes the movement disorder DYT1 primary dystonia (Ozelius et al., 1997; Breakefield et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Humans have four Torsin orthologs: TorsinA, TorsinB, Torsin2A, and Torsin3A.
source: Deletion of a single glutamate in TorsinA (humans have four Torsin orthologs: TorsinA, TorsinB, Torsin2A, and Torsin3A) at position 302/303 causes the movement disorder DYT1 primary dystonia (Ozelius et al., 1997; Breakefield et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about human Torsin proteins.

claim: LAP1 and LULL1 were first considered as Torsin substrates.
source: While LAP1 and LULL1 were first considered as Torsin substrates (Naismith et al., 2009), they are now being proposed as possible activators of Torsin (Zhao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: LAP1 and LULL1 are now being proposed as possible activators of Torsin.
source: While LAP1 and LULL1 were first considered as Torsin substrates (Naismith et al., 2009), they are now being proposed as possible activators of Torsin (Zhao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature and the data presented in this manuscript.

claim: LAP1 and LULL1 can both form heterohexameric ring assemblies with Torsin.
source: Our data suggest that LAP1 and LULL1 can both form heterohexameric ring assemblies with Torsin, whereby Torsin is activated through an arginine finger at amino acid (aa) R563 of LAP1 (R449 of LULL1).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy and modeling data.

claim: Torsin is activated through an arginine finger at amino acid R563 of LAP1.
source: Our data suggest that LAP1 and LULL1 can both form heterohexameric ring assemblies with Torsin, whereby Torsin is activated through an arginine finger at amino acid (aa) R563 of LAP1 (R449 of LULL1).
evidence: This is supported by ATPase activity assays and structural modeling.

claim: Torsin is activated through an arginine finger at amino acid R449 of LULL1.
source: Our data suggest that LAP1 and LULL1 can both form heterohexameric ring assemblies with Torsin, whereby Torsin is activated through an arginine finger at amino acid (aa) R563 of LAP1 (R449 of LULL1).
evidence: This is supported by ATPase activity assays and structural modeling.

claim: LAP1 and LULL1 each have dual roles, namely the targeting and activation of Torsins.
source: Thus LAP1 and LULL1 each have dual roles, namely the targeting and activation of Torsins.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and biochemical data presented.

claim: The conserved luminal domain of LAP1 (aa356–583) was recombinantly expressed, purified, and set up for crystallization.
source: The conserved luminal domain of LAP1 (aa356–583) was recombinantly expressed, purified, and set up for crystallization.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used.

claim: A camelid single domain (VHH) antibody fragment, VHH-BS1, was produced against LAP1 as a crystallization chaperone.
source: Because the protein failed to yield crystals alone, we produced a camelid single domain (VHH) antibody fragment, VHH-BS1, against LAP1 as a crystallization chaperone.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used.

claim: The complex of VHH-BS1 and LAP1 yielded well-diffracting crystals.
source: The complex of VHH-BS1 and LAP1 yielded well-diffracting crystals (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data in Table 1.

claim: The structure was solved using molecular replacement with VHH as the search model.
source: The structure was solved using molecular replacement with VHH as the search model (for details, see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This describes the method used for structure determination.

claim: In the asymmetric unit there are two LAP1 molecules related by a non-crystallographic symmetry axis, each identically bound by one VHH.
source: In the asymmetric unit we find two LAP1 molecules related by a non-crystallographic symmetry axis, each identically bound by one VHH.
evidence: This describes the crystal structure content.

claim: The final structure is completely built, except for four N-terminal residues in LAP1, which seem disordered in the crystal.
source: The final structure is completely built, except for four N-terminal residues in LAP1, which seem disordered in the crystal (six N-terminal residues in the second LAP1 copy).
evidence: This describes the completeness of the structural model.

claim: The D2 domain of the two-ring AAA+ ATPase ClpB superimposes on LAP1 with an rmsd of 3.28 Å over 111 Cα positions.
source: The D2 domain of the two-ring AAA+ ATPase ClpB superimposes on LAP1 with an rmsd of 3.28 Å over 111 Cα positions (Figure 1; Zeymer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a quantitative structural comparison.

claim: ClpB belongs to the additional strand conserved E (ASCE) family.
source: ClpB belongs to the additional strand conserved E (ASCE) family (Iyer et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: Like ASCE-type AAA+ proteins, LAP1 has a central, five-stranded parallel β-sheet, surrounded on both sides by 10 helices in total.
source: Like ASCE-type AAA+ proteins, such as ClpA, ClpB, and p97, LAP1 also has a central, five-stranded parallel β-sheet, surrounded on both sides by 10 helices in total (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the crystal structure shown in Figure 1.

claim: The secondary structure topology of LAP1 is α(−1)α(0)β1α(1)β2-α(2a)α(2b)β3α(3a)α(3b)β4α(4)β5α(5)α(6).
source: The secondary structure topology is α(−1)α(0)β1α(1)β2-α(2a)α(2b)β3α(3a)α(3b)β4α(4)β5α(5)α(6), using the AAA+ nomenclature (Erzberger and Berger, 2006).
evidence: This is determined from the crystal structure.

claim: In contrast to canonical ASCE-type ATPases, LAP1 lacks a C-terminal domain.
source: In contrast to canonical ASCE-type ATPases (Figure 1C), LAP1 lacks a C-terminal domain.
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural comparison in Figure 1.

claim: The C terminus of LAP1 is attached to helix α1 via a disulfide bond between the highly conserved residues C424 and C582.
source: Instead the C terminus is attached to helix α1 via a disulfide bond between the highly conserved residues C424 and C582 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In a AAA+ ATPase, the nucleotide binding pocket is the most sequence-conserved region, defined by the essential Walker A and B motifs.
source: In a AAA+ ATPase, the nucleotide binding pocket is the most sequence-conserved region, defined by the essential Walker A and B motifs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AAA+ ATPases.

claim: LAP1 lacks a recognizable Walker A region.
source: LAP1 lacks a recognizable Walker A region, typically located between β1 and α1 (Figure 2A,B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence and structural analysis shown in Figures 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Helix α1 in LAP1 is N-terminally extended compared to AAA+ ATPases, thereby sterically blocking the nucleotide-binding pocket.
source: Instead, helix α1 is N-terminally extended compared to AAA+ ATPases, thereby sterically blocking the nucleotide-binding pocket.
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison.

claim: The Walker B motif with the canonical sequence hhhhDE is instead hhhhHR in human LAP1, and therefore cannot interact with nucleotide.
source: The Walker B motif with the canonical sequence hhhhDE (h, hydrophobic), is instead hhhhHR in human LAP1, and therefore cannot interact with nucleotide.
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence analysis and structural inference.

claim: The conserved disulfide bridge in LAP1 would interfere with nucleotide binding.
source: Finally, the conserved disulfide bridge would also interfere with nucleotide binding (Figure 2B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural position of the disulfide bridge.

claim: The four canonical nucleotide-sensing elements, Walker A, Walker B, Sensor 1, and Sensor 2, are well conserved and immediately recognizable in TorsinA when compared to ClpB-D2.
source: The four canonical nucleotide-sensing elements, Walker A, Walker B, Sensor 1, and Sensor 2 (Erzberger and Berger, 2006), are well conserved and immediately recognizable in TorsinA when compared to ClpB-D2 (Figure 2C,D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Kock et al., 2006; Zhu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence alignment and modeling shown in Figures 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: AAA+ ATPases are often activated by an arginine residue ('arginine finger') in the neighboring protomer in the hexameric ring assembly.
source: AAA+ ATPases are often activated by an arginine residue ('arginine finger') in the neighboring protomer in the hexameric ring assembly, such that this arginine is positioned to reach the phosphate binding site (Wendler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: There is no conserved arginine in TorsinA at the expected position at the end of helix α5.
source: While we do not find a conserved arginine in TorsinA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) at the expected position at the end of helix α5, in LAP1 this residue is a strictly conserved arginine (R563).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence alignment in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In LAP1, the residue at the position corresponding to the arginine finger is a strictly conserved arginine (R563).
source: While we do not find a conserved arginine in TorsinA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) at the expected position at the end of helix α5, in LAP1 this residue is a strictly conserved arginine (R563).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence alignment and structural analysis.

claim: Modeling and phylogenetic analysis strongly suggest that LAP1 and TorsinA might form a heterohexameric ring with three active sites in which TorsinA and its partner subunits alternate to form the ring.
source: Consequently, modeling and phylogenetic analysis strongly suggest that LAP1 and TorsinA might form a heterohexameric ring (Figure 3A,B) with three active sites in which TorsinA and its partner subunits alternate to form the ring.
evidence: This is based on structural modeling and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: LAP1 and LULL1 activate TorsinA in vitro.
source: This hypothesis is further strengthened by the recent observation that LAP1 and LULL1 activate TorsinA in vitro (Zhao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature and the ATPase assays in this manuscript.

claim: TorsinA(E171Q):LAP1 and TorsinA(E171Q):LULL1 complexes were obtained with 1:1 stoichiometry.
source: We obtained complexes with TorsinA(E171Q):LAP1 and TorsinA(E171Q):LULL1 1:1 stoichiometry (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by size exclusion chromatography and SDS-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The E171Q mutation traps TorsinA in the ATP-bound form, which helps to stabilize the interaction with LAP1 and LULL1.
source: The E171Q mutation traps TorsinA in the ATP-bound form, which helps to stabilize the interaction with LAP1 and LULL1, respectively (Goodchild and Dauer, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Rings of expected size were observed for the TorsinA(E171Q):LAP1 and TorsinA(E171Q):LULL1 complex preparations, but not for individually purified LAP1(356–583) or LULL1(322–570).
source: On individual micrographs, rings of expected size were observed for the two-complex preparation, but not for individually purified LAP1(356–583) or LULL1(322–570) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy images in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: TorsinA(E171Q) is insoluble without binding partner.
source: TorsinA(E171Q) is insoluble without binding partner, therefore the observed rings should not be homomeric (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by precipitation experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Class averaging of 808 TorsinA(E171Q):LULL1 particles yielded multiple classes showing ring assembly.
source: Class averaging of 808 TorsinA(E171Q):LULL1 particles yielded multiple classes showing ring assembly (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The rings have a diameter of ∼120 Å, in good agreement with typical hexameric AAA+ ATPase assemblies.
source: The rings have a diameter of ∼120 Å, in good agreement with typical hexameric AAA+ ATPase assemblies.
evidence: This is measured from electron microscopy images and compared to known structures.

claim: The mutants TorsinA:LAP1(R563A) and TorsinA:LULL1(R449A) showed substantial reduction in ATPase activity compared to wild-type TorsinA:LAP1.
source: In comparison to wild-type TorsinA:LAP1, the mutants TorsinA:LAP1(R563A) and TorsinA:LULL1(R449A) showed substantial reduction in ATPase activity, while both TorsinA(E171Q):LAP1 and TorsinA(E171Q):LULL1 are essentially inactive (Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ATPase activity assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: TorsinA(E171Q):LAP1 and TorsinA(E171Q):LULL1 are essentially inactive.
source: In comparison to wild-type TorsinA:LAP1, the mutants TorsinA:LAP1(R563A) and TorsinA:LULL1(R449A) showed substantial reduction in ATPase activity, while both TorsinA(E171Q):LAP1 and TorsinA(E171Q):LULL1 are essentially inactive (Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ATPase activity assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: The ATP hydrolysis rates are very slow.
source: We note that the ATP hydrolysis rates are very slow and that the effect of the arginine finger mutation is not as drastic as seen with other AAA+ ATPases.
evidence: This is observed from the ATPase activity assays.

claim: The effect of the arginine finger mutation is not as drastic as seen with other AAA+ ATPases.
source: We note that the ATP hydrolysis rates are very slow and that the effect of the arginine finger mutation is not as drastic as seen with other AAA+ ATPases.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with other AAA+ ATPases.

claim: The ATP hydrolysis rate in the presence of substrate is likely higher.
source: We speculate that the ATP hydrolysis rate in the presence of substrate is likely higher, and that the effect of the arginine finger is likely more pronounced in a more physiological context.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed data.

claim: The effect of the arginine finger is likely more pronounced in a more physiological context.
source: We speculate that the ATP hydrolysis rate in the presence of substrate is likely higher, and that the effect of the arginine finger is likely more pronounced in a more physiological context.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed data.

claim: LAP1 and LULL1 both activate Torsins by providing the arginine finger in a heterohexameric ring assembly in which LAP1 and LULL1 alternate with Torsin.
source: In summary, we conclude that LAP1 and LULL1 both activate Torsins by providing the arginine finger in a heterohexameric ring assembly in which LAP1 and LULL1 alternate with Torsin.
evidence: This is the main conclusion based on all the structural and biochemical data presented.

claim: LAP1 and LULL1 contain transmembrane helices immediately N-terminal to their luminal, nucleotide-free AAA+ Activator domain.
source: Since LAP1 and LULL1 contain transmembrane helices immediately N-terminal to their luminal, nucleotide-free AAA+ Activator domain, they bring Torsin into close proximity to the membrane (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on known protein architecture and illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: LAP1 and LULL1 bring Torsin into close proximity to the membrane.
source: Since LAP1 and LULL1 contain transmembrane helices immediately N-terminal to their luminal, nucleotide-free AAA+ Activator domain, they bring Torsin into close proximity to the membrane (Figure 5).
evidence: This is inferred from the protein architecture and illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: A heterohexameric ring assembly for AAA+ ATPases is unusual, but not unprecedented.
source: A heterohexameric ring assembly for AAA+ ATPases is unusual, but not unprecedented (Gribun et al., 2008; Saffian et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: This is the first description of a heterohexameric assembly where a canonical AAA+ domain alternates with a nucleotide-free AAA+ like domain.
source: However, to our knowledge this is the first description of a heterohexameric assembly where a canonical AAA+ domain alternates with a nucleotide-free AAA+ like domain, which we now call AAA+ Activator domain.
evidence: This is a novel finding from this study.

claim: The nucleotide-free AAA+ like domain is now called AAA+ Activator domain.
source: However, to our knowledge this is the first description of a heterohexameric assembly where a canonical AAA+ domain alternates with a nucleotide-free AAA+ like domain, which we now call AAA+ Activator domain.
evidence: This is a new nomenclature proposed by the authors.

claim: LAP1 and LULL1 lack all canonical nucleotide-binding elements.
source: It is striking that LAP1 and LULL1 lack all canonical nucleotide-binding elements.
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural and sequence analysis.

claim: The lack of canonical nucleotide-binding elements has complicated the detection of LAP1 and LULL1 by sequence-based methods.
source: This feature has undoubtedly complicated their detection by sequence-based methods.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural findings.

claim: Using the LAP1 structure, a reverse hidden Markov model search identified Torsins as the top hits besides LAP1 homologs.
source: Using the LAP1 structure, we performed a reverse hidden Markov model search to possibly identify structurally similar proteins in various organisms using Backphyre (Kelley and Sternberg, 2009). Interestingly, the top hits that we find besides LAP1 homologs are the Torsins.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis.

claim: LAP1 and Torsins are possibly derived from a common ancestor.
source: This indicates that both proteins are possibly derived from a common ancestor.
evidence: This is inferred from the bioinformatic analysis.

claim: LAP1 homologs are found in Drosophila and Caenorhabditis that have so far escaped detection.
source: In Drosophila as well as in Caenorhabditis, we find LAP1 homologs that have so far escaped detection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence alignment in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: For all species where an orphaned Torsin has been found, a LAP1/LULL1 homolog is now also found.
source: Gratifyingly, for all species where so far an orphaned Torsin has been found, we now also find a LAP1/LULL1 homolog (for many species, it is difficult to distinguish between LAP1 and LULL1 based on sequence alone).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: VHH-BS1 binds to the area immediately surrounding the arginine finger of LAP1, thereby interfering with TorsinA binding.
source: We note that VHH-BS1 binds to the area immediately surrounding the arginine finger of LAP1, thereby interfering with TorsinA binding (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the crystal structure and competition experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: VHH-BS1 can compete with LAP1 for TorsinA binding in vitro.
source: Interestingly, VHH-BS1 can compete with LAP1 for TorsinA binding in vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by precipitation experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Torsin acts in close proximity to the NE or the ER membrane, depending on whether it interacts with membrane-bound LAP1 or LULL1, respectively.
source: Torsin acts in close proximity to the NE or the ER membrane, depending on whether it interacts with membrane-bound LAP1 or LULL1, respectively.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization of LAP1 and LULL1.

claim: Membrane proximity is further ensured by the N-terminal hydrophobic region within TorsinA.
source: Membrane proximity is further ensured by the N-terminal hydrophobic region within TorsinA (Vander Heyden et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: TorsinA is involved in the exit of large ribonucleoprotein (mRNP) granules from the nucleus through a pathway akin to the nuclear egress of herpes-type viruses.
source: Using an ATP-trapped mutant, it was shown that TorsinA is involved in the exit of large ribonucleoprotein (mRNP) granules from the nucleus through a pathway akin to the nuclear egress of herpes-type viruses (Rose and Schlieker, 2012; Speese et al., 2012; Jokhi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: A substrate-trap mutant of TorsinA localized to the neck of mRNP-filled vesicles that bud from the inner nuclear membrane (INM) into the perinuclear space.
source: A substrate-trap mutant of TorsinA localized to the neck of mRNP-filled vesicles that bud from the inner nuclear membrane (INM) into the perinuclear space (Jokhi et al., 2013), consistent with our model of LAP1-mediated activation of TorsinA close to the INM.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The elusive Torsin substrates include proteins involved in membrane scission.
source: We therefore speculate that the so far elusive Torsin substrates include proteins involved in membrane scission.
evidence: This is speculation based on the localization and function data.

claim: The action of Torsin is akin to the AAA+ ATPase Vps4 involved in the scission of narrow membrane necks mediated by ESCRT-III components.
source: This is akin to the action of the AAA+ ATPase Vps4 involved in the scission of narrow membrane necks mediated by ESCRT-III (endosomal sorting complexes required for transport) components (Hill and Babst, 2012; McCullough et al., 2013), but with an important difference: while Vps4 acts on the inside of the necks, Torsins presumably act on the outside.
evidence: This is speculation based on comparison with known systems.

claim: While Vps4 acts on the inside of membrane necks, Torsins presumably act on the outside.
source: This is akin to the action of the AAA+ ATPase Vps4 involved in the scission of narrow membrane necks mediated by ESCRT-III (endosomal sorting complexes required for transport) components (Hill and Babst, 2012; McCullough et al., 2013), but with an important difference: while Vps4 acts on the inside of the necks, Torsins presumably act on the outside.
evidence: This is speculation based on the proposed model.

claim: Under more physiological conditions, the ATPase activity of Torsin might be substantially higher than that reported under the in vitro conditions tested so far.
source: We further speculate that under more physiological conditions, that is, properly complexed with LAP1 or LULL1 and engaged with substrate, the ATPase activity of Torsin might be substantially higher than that reported under the in vitro conditions tested so far.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed low activity in vitro.

claim: Understanding the catalytic mechanism of the Torsin-LAP1/LULL1 machinery is important.
source: Apart from the identification of Torsin substrate(s), understanding the catalytic mechanism of the Torsin-LAP1/LULL1 machinery is equally important.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Substantial differences are expected between the Torsin-LAP1/LULL1 system and better understood AAA+ systems because of the unusual heterohexameric architecture with only three active sites.
source: Because of the unusual heterohexameric architecture with only three active sites, we expect substantial differences between this system and those that are better understood.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural findings.

claim: Both LAP1/LULL1 and Torsin have conserved cysteines.
source: While both proteins have conserved disulfides, these do not account for all cysteines and suggest a possible redox mechanism, as has been discussed previously (Zhu et al., 2010, 2008).
evidence: This is observed from sequence analysis and cited literature.

claim: The conserved cysteines suggest a possible redox mechanism.
source: While both proteins have conserved disulfides, these do not account for all cysteines and suggest a possible redox mechanism, as has been discussed previously (Zhu et al., 2010, 2008).
evidence: This is speculation based on sequence analysis and cited literature.

claim: The most conserved cysteine C496 in LAP1 cannot engage in an intramolecular disulfide bridge.
source: We note that in our model the most conserved cysteine C496 in LAP1 cannot engage in an intramolecular disulfide bridge, but is close to the nucleotide-binding site of the neighboring TorsinA.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural model.

claim: The most conserved cysteine C496 in LAP1 is close to the nucleotide-binding site of the neighboring TorsinA.
source: We note that in our model the most conserved cysteine C496 in LAP1 cannot engage in an intramolecular disulfide bridge, but is close to the nucleotide-binding site of the neighboring TorsinA.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural model.

claim: The conservation of C496 might indicate a role in a redox mechanism that is coupled to the catalytic cycle of Torsin-LAP1/LULL1.
source: This remarkable conservation might indicate a role in a redox mechanism that is coupled to the catalytic cycle of Torsin-LAP1/LULL1.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural position and conservation of C496.

claim: The lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum is a site rich in oxidoreductases that assist in protein folding and assembly.
source: The lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum is a site rich in oxidoreductases that assist in protein folding and assembly.
